gold.abstract: Participation incentives is a well-known issue inhibiting randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in medicine, as well as a potential cause of user dissatisfaction for RCTs in online platforms. We frame this issue as a non-standard exploration-exploitation tradeoff: an RCT would like to explore as uniformly as possible, whereas each "agent" (a patient or a user) prefers "exploitation", i.e., treatments that seem best. We incentivize participation by leveraging information asymmetry between the trial and the agents. We measure statistical performance via worst-case estimation error under adversarially generated outcomes, a standard objective for RCTs. We obtain a near-optimal solution in terms of this objective: an incentive-compatible mechanism with a particular guarantee, and a nearly matching impossibility result for any incentive-compatible mechanism. We consider three model variants: homogeneous agents (of the same "type" comprising beliefs and preferences), heterogeneous agents, and an extension that leverages estimated type frequencies to mitigate the influence of rare-but-difficult agent types.

Research task:
Develop a feasible and novel interdisciplinary research idea that genuinely integrates the two source papers. Specify the cross-disciplinary mechanism, a testable research design, and the contribution beyond either paper alone.

Source papers available to you:

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper C: Conjoint analysis with 108 AD study partners shows home visits provide the highest utility (0.89) and can offset high intervention risk disutility (-0.85). Car service adds little beyond home visits. Willingness to participate rises from 17% (amenities only) to 27% (home visits) to 60% (low risk + high chance of active treatment). Hassle reduction correlates with patient ADL severity (r=0.41) and NPI score (r=0.24).

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Paper C’s home-visit utility can be causally linked to reduced caregiver travel burden and patient ADL severity. I propose using caregiver-reported daily travel time as the mediating variable: home visits eliminate travel, which is most valuable when patient ADL impairment makes transport physically demanding. This connects Paper C’s preference data to a measurable behavioral mechanism (travel time saved) that can be tested prospectively.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Recruit 200 AD study partners (caregivers) stratified by patient ADL severity (mild vs. moderate/severe). Measure baseline weekly travel time for any clinical activity. Randomize partners to view two trial scenarios: (1) standard clinic visits, (2) home visits. Use discrete choice experiment with risk and active-treatment chance fixed at moderate levels. Primary outcome: stated willingness to enroll (yes/no). Mediation analysis: test whether travel time saved explains the effect of home visits on willingness, and whether this mediation is stronger in high ADL-severity dyads. Validate stated willingness against a 2-week follow-up where partners are offered a mock enrollment for a real observational study with home or clinic visits.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
Alzheimer’s trial recruitment suffers from caregiver burden. Prior conjoint data show home visits strongly increase willingness to participate, but the mechanism is untested. We hypothesize that home visits work by reducing caregiver travel time, and that this effect is amplified when patient ADL impairment makes transport difficult. A stratified discrete choice experiment with 200 caregivers will test whether travel time saved mediates the home-visit effect on enrollment willingness, with a behavioral validation follow-up. This moves from preference measurement to a causal, mechanism-based recruitment intervention.

FINAL IDEA: Home visits increase Alzheimer trial enrollment by reducing caregiver travel time, with the effect strongest for dyads with high patient ADL impairment—a testable causal mechanism derived from conjoint preference data.

Adaptive trials can change allocation ratios or add arms mid-study, but these changes may alter the perceived trial attributes (risk, home visits, active treatment chance) that Paper C shows drive enrollment. I propose a causal feedback loop: use Paper C's utility weights to predict how each adaptive design change shifts caregiver willingness to enroll, then constrain the adaptation algorithm to avoid changes that would drop predicted enrollment below a pre-specified threshold. This connects behavioral preference measurement (Paper C) to adaptive trial methodology (Researcher A's domain) through a measurable, operational mechanism: predicted enrollment utility as a constraint on adaptation decisions.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Simulation study using Paper C's published utility weights and variance estimates. Generate 10,000 virtual AD trial scenarios with adaptive designs (e.g., response-adaptive randomization, arm dropping). For each adaptation step, compute predicted caregiver enrollment probability using Paper C's conjoint model (home visits, risk, active treatment chance). Compare three conditions: (1) unconstrained adaptive design, (2) adaptive design with enrollment-utility constraint (predicted willingness ≥ 40%), (3) fixed design with home visits. Primary outcomes: type I error rate, power, and predicted enrollment over time. Validation: compare predicted enrollment against Paper C's observed willingness proportions (17%, 27%, 60%) using posterior predictive checks. Sensitivity analysis: vary ADL severity distribution and risk tolerance using Paper C's reported correlations.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
Adaptive trials risk population drift and type I error inflation, but current methodology ignores how design changes alter caregiver willingness to enroll. We integrate conjoint-derived enrollment utilities from Alzheimer's trial partners into an adaptive design simulation framework. A constrained adaptation algorithm maintains predicted enrollment above threshold while preserving statistical validity. Simulation across 10,000 scenarios compares unconstrained adaptive, enrollment-constrained adaptive, and fixed home-visit designs. This provides the first operational bridge between behavioral trial recruitment science and adaptive design theory, yielding a practical tool for trialists.

FINAL IDEA: Adaptive trial designs can be algorithmically constrained using conjoint-derived caregiver enrollment utilities to prevent adaptation-induced recruitment collapse while controlling type I error—a mechanism integrating behavioral economics with adaptive methodology.
